note: Subject–Object–Verb: 'I water drink.' The 을 on 물 is a tag that says 'this is the thing being acted on' — which is why Korean can shuffle words and still make sense.
밥 is literally cooked rice but stands in for food and meals in general — eating 밥 just means eating.
'Like' is a verb here (좋아하다), so it goes to the end like any other verb, and the thing you like takes the object tag 를.
공부하다 is 공부 (studying) + 하다 (do) — 'to do studying.' Every ~하다 verb ends in 해요 in the polite form.
가 marks 친구 as the do-er. 'To' isn't a separate word in front — it's the particle 에 glued onto the back of 학교.
Same frame as going to school — swap the place, keep the skeleton. Korean present tense covers English 'go' and 'am going' both.
있다 means 'to exist' — so this is both 'there's water' and 'I have water.' Korean has no separate everyday verb for having; things just exist (for you).
A structure with no English twin: Korean says 'time not-exists' rather than 'I don't have time.' The owner (me) is simply understood and dropped — Korean omits anything obvious from context.
맛있다 is literally 맛 (taste) + 있다 (exists) — 'taste exists.' Describing words are verbs in Korean, so no 'is' is needed.
The same sentence as 'I drink water' with one swap: 친구가 instead of 저는. The particles do the work; the verb never changes for the subject.
The subject stays first — it's the VERB that moves to the end. And 'to' isn't a separate word in front; it's the particle 에 glued onto the back of 가게 (store).
Same skeleton with a different subject: 가 marks 친구 as the do-er, 를 marks 커피 as the thing liked, verb caps it off.

Four pieces now: subject, then place, then object, then verb. 에서 (not just 에) marks where an action happens — a small preview of Module 2. Typical order is S–Place–O–V, but the particles do the real work.
Same pattern as 'I go to the store' — swap the pieces, keep the skeleton. This is why learning the frame once pays off forever.
Your first past tense: 만나다 → drop 다, last vowel is ㅏ so add 았어요 → 만났어요. The subject is understood and simply dropped.
에 marks time too — 아침에 'in the morning'. 먹다's stem vowel is ㅓ, so the past is 먹었어요.
Actions happen with 에서, not 에 — the cafe is the venue, not the destination. 마시다 → 마셨어요.
The S–Place–O–V frame you previewed in Module 1 (학교에서), now official: 에서 marks where the studying happens.
도 doesn't stack on 을/를 — it replaces it. 음악을도 is wrong; 음악도 carries both 'object' and 'also' at once.
하고 glued to a noun means 'with'. 보다 contracts in the past: 보 + 았어요 → 봤어요.
Destinations keep 에 even in the past. 가다 → 갔어요 — the ㅏ stem and 았 merge into one syllable.
회사 is literally 'company', but 회사에서 일해요 is just 'I'm at work'. 일하다 = 일 (work) + 하다 (do) → 일해요.
The present tense covers the near future — 내일 만나요 needs no 'will'. The time word does the work.
하고 between nouns is 'and' — and only the last noun in the list takes 을/를. 사다 → 샀어요.
듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel ending, ㄷ softens to ㄹ — 들어요, 들었어요. A small family of verbs (걷다 'walk', 묻다 'ask') does the same.
Time-에 once more: 주말에 'on the weekend'. Time words like to lead the sentence, before even the subject.
맵다 → 매워요: the ㅂ softens to 워 before a vowel. A whole family of ㅂ-adjectives does this — file the shape, the full rule comes later.
Negation is one tiny word: 안 sits directly before the verb. No do-support, no word-order gymnastics — 안 먹어요, done.
못 is 안's cousin with a different meaning: not won't — CAN'T. 안 마셔요 is a choice; 못 마셔요 is ability or circumstance.
Wanting bolts onto the verb stem: 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요. Any verb works — drop 다, add 고 싶어요.
The Module 2 pattern with the new meal word: time-에 up front, past tense at the end.
Everything recycled from Module 2 in one breath: action-place 에서, noun-joining 하고, past 샀어요.
만들다 → 만들었어요. The S–O–V skeleton hasn't changed since your first sentence — only the bricks get richer.
-고 싶어요 again with a new verb: 시키다 → 시키고 싶어요. 시키다 is the everyday word for ordering in.
The 없어요 pattern from Module 1, mid-recipe: 'sugar not-exists' = we're out of sugar.
Describing words are verbs, so tastes conjugate like actions: 짜다 → 짜요, 달다 → 달아요.
배고프다 → 배고파요: the ㅡ drops before 아. You met this sentence's soul in the gap deck — 'stomach is hungry.'
싫어하다 is 좋아하다's opposite and works identically: the disliked thing takes 을/를, the verb caps the sentence.
Module 2's 식당 finally gets its sentence. 주문하다 is the proper restaurant word; 시키다 is its casual twin.
One word, whole sentence — subject understood, 배부르다 → 배불러요 (a 르-irregular; just bank this form). The natural end of any good meal.
우리 가족 — 'our family' even when you mean yours alone. And 살다 takes 에, not 에서: where you live is where you exist, not where you act.
The copula glues onto the noun itself: 선생님 + 이에요. After a consonant it's 이에요; after a vowel, 예요.
The same sentence one register up: 입니다 is the 합니다-style copula. Say it in interviews and introductions; say 학생이에요 everywhere else.
The -(으)시- honorific hides inside 오세요 (오 + 시 + 어요). It elevates the SUBJECT — you use it about respected people, never about yourself.
Honorifics don't just add 시 — some verbs get replaced outright. Elders don't 먹다; they 드시다.
-(으)시- works on describing words too: 바쁘다 → 바쁘세요. Your own parents get honorifics when you talk about them.
Not-knowing is its own verb — 모르다, not 안 알다. 르-irregular: 몰라요, like 배불러요.
A Module 2 sentence promoted to the 합니다 style: 일해요 → 일합니다. Same meaning, more starch — this is self-introduction register.
가수 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 예요 (not 이에요). And 오빠 tells you the speaker is female — sibling words carry the speaker's gender.
Inside the family, casual words and plain 해요체 are normal — 아빠 cooks; 아버지 would 요리하세요 in front of guests.
반말, mechanically: 가요 minus the 요. That's the whole trick — but only with close friends, younger family, or kids.
Another vowel-final noun, another 예요. 언니 marks the speaker as female — a male speaker would say 누나는 의사예요.
Module 2's 하고-'with' at the family table. 밥을 먹다 is such a unit that it rides in the verb chunk here — eating rice is just eating.
있다's honorific replacement: respected people don't 있다, they 계시다. With 우리 집 — 'our house' — doing its warm Korean thing.
몇 + counter is the question machine: 몇 시 (what hour), 몇 명 (how many people), 몇 살 (how old). The copula rides on the counter.
The hybrid clock in one sentence: hours take native numbers (세 시), minutes take Sino (십 분). Every Korean clock-reading mixes both systems.
반 (half) replaces 삼십 분 the way 'half past' replaces 'thirty' — and 오전/오후 go BEFORE the time, not after.
The counting frame: [thing] [number] [counter] — 커피 두 잔, never 두 커피. The object particle usually drops off counted phrases in speech.
Age = native number + 살 + copula. 열 keeps its full form — only 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 contract before counters.
A normal early question in Korea — age decides speech register (Module 4!), so it's practical, not rude. To an elder, upgrade the noun: 연세가 어떻게 되세요?
How Koreans state family size: 'our family is four people.' 넷 contracts to 네 before the people-counter 명.
마리 counts animals — including the ones you're about to cook. Two fish at the market: 생선 두 마리.
Same counting frame inside a full Module 2 past-tense sentence. The pieces keep composing — that's the whole course thesis.
읽다 finally in action: 읽었어요 — the buried ㄹ surfaces (il-geo-sseo-yo). 셋 → 세 before the counter.
Days take time-에 like 아침 and 주말 did. Two 에s in one sentence, doing two jobs — time and destination.
Module 4's copula welding two Module 5 nouns. 금요일 + 이에요 — the day itself takes no particle here.
The 있어요-have pattern from Module 1: plans exist (for me). 약속 있어요 is the standard 'I've got plans' — see the gap deck for why it's not a solemn vow.
하나 → 한 before its counter, the most common contraction of all: 한 잔, 한 명, 한 개. 매일 needs no particle — it's self-sufficiently adverbial.
The single most useful sentence in this course. 어디 sits exactly where the answer will: 화장실이 [어디]에 있어요? → [저기]에 있어요.
The location frame: [thing]은/는 [landmark] [position]에 있어요. Position words are NOUNS — 병원 옆 is literally 'the hospital's side.'
Position 안 (inside) after the noun — not to be confused with negation 안, which stands before a verb. Same sound, opposite neighborhoods.
'On' = 위에, 'the desk's topside-at.' English prepositions come BEFORE; Korean position nouns come AFTER, then 에 seals the phrase.
(으)로 marks a HEADING, not a destination — 왼쪽으로 is 'leftward.' Compare 학교에 가요 (to school, the endpoint) with 학교로 가요 (in the school's direction).
(으)로's second job: means. 지하철로 = by subway. After ㄹ it's bare 로 — 지하철로, not 지하철으로.

rom: ojeon ahop sibuteo ohu yeoseot sikkaji ilhaeyo
note: The time bracket: 부터 opens it, 까지 closes it. Everything inside is Module 5 — the course is compounding.
The space bracket: 에서 opens it (from), 까지 closes it (as far as). And 걷다 is a ㄷ-irregular like 듣다: 걸어요.
There-is and location are one pattern in Korean: 'park exists at house's front' covers both 'there's a park in front' and 'the park is in front.'
Same frame, new position noun. Swap 옆/앞/뒤/위/아래 in and out — the skeleton never moves.
가깝다 → 가까워요, the same ㅂ-softening as 맵다 → 매워요. Its partner 멀다 stays regular: 멀어요.
The magic taxi words. Getting off happens FROM a place, so 여기 takes 에서 — the action-location particle earning its keep.

en.t: between the bank and the supermarket

note: 사이 (the between-space) is a noun like every position word: A하고 B 사이에 = 'at A-and-B's between.'
What you ride is a direct object in Korean: 버스를 타요, 'ride the bus.' Compare 지하철로 가요, where the subway is the means, not the thing acted on.
The load-bearing wall of small talk. Any 하다-adjective conjugates like the verb: 따뜻하다 → 따뜻해요.
-지만 welds 'but' onto the first verb: drop 다, add 지만. Only the final verb carries the politeness 요 — the welded one travels light.
Connectives open the NEXT sentence: cause, full stop, 그래서, result. Your first two-sentence unit — this is what talking actually sounds like.
Division of labor: 하고 joins nouns inside a sentence; 그리고 joins whole sentences. With Module 2's 도 tagging along.
The truest sentence in this course. 그런데 is the soft pivot; 어렵다 goes ㅂ-irregular: 어려워요.
-지만 on a Module 4 adjective, no subject needed. Note 바쁘지만 keeps the ㅡ — the drop only happens before 아/어, and 지만 starts with ㅈ.
Colors are nouns ([hue] + 색), so they take the copula: 빨간색이에요, 'is red-color.' The Module 4 machine keeps paying rent.
Module 1's 예쁘다 returns with its ㅡ-drop showing: 예뻐요. The 슬프다/바쁘다/배고프다 family keeps growing.
Subject and object both understood — context carries everything, the verb carries the feeling. The most famous dropped-subject sentence in Korean.
Feelings are stated body-outward, like 배고프다: not 'I feel good' but 'the mood is good.' The self is implied, the state is the subject.
The ㅡ-drop in the past: 슬프다 → 슬펐어요. Both sentences in past tense — Korean keeps the timeline consistent across the 그래서.
하지만 is the firm 'but' — a real contrast follows. 듣다's ㄷ-irregular from Module 2 rides again: 들어요.
The Swiss-army sentence. As a question: are you okay? As an answer: I'm fine — or no thanks. The gap deck sorts out its three jobs.
Module 1's 시간이 없어요, answered at last. 많다 → 많아요, the ㅎ falling silent — abundance stated the same exist-style way as lack.
Clock times take 에, like every time expression — and it's the native number before 시, exactly as Module 5 drilled.
No 'my' needed — whose hands would they be? Korean drops possessives the way it drops subjects: anything obvious goes unsaid.
Meet 이 the tooth — same syllable as 이 (two) and the subject particle. The gap deck throws a small party for this overworked sound.
The progressive: verb stem + 고 있어요. 있다 moonlights again — this time as 'be in the middle of.' The classic phone answer to 뭐 해요?
No 'for' — what you await is a plain direct object: 친구를 기다려요. English prepositions keep dissolving into Korean particles.
The future: stem + -(으)ㄹ 거예요. 쉬다 ends in a vowel, so the ㄹ hooks straight on: 쉴 거예요. Resting is an action, so home takes 에서.
Every 하다 verb futures the same way: 하다 → 할 거예요. And 방 finally enters the vocabulary — Father can now enter the room officially.
Consonant stems take the full 을: 먹을 거예요. Both futures in one pattern — ㄹ after vowels, 을 after consonants, 거예요 always.

rom: botong jihacheoreul tayo. geureonde oneureun georeoyo
note: 오늘은 — the topic particle marking a CONTRAST: 'as for today (unlike usual).' 은/는's second job, quietly doing what English does with stress.
The frequency ladder slots in before the place and verb: 항상 (always) > 보통 (usually) > 자주 (often) > 가끔 (sometimes).
끝나다 — the thing ends by itself, no one ending it. And 여덟 시 puts Module 5's trickiest number straight to work.
Nouns stack directly: 주말 계획, 'weekend plans.' The 있어요-have pattern asks the Friday-afternoon question of every office.
Adjectives take the future too — 바쁠 거예요. On adjectives and other people it shades toward 'probably': the gap deck covers the blur.
하다 as 'to play' — games, like studying and work, are things you DO. Module 1's do-everything verb keeps collecting jobs.
